keep away: stay away from someone or something
typical: keep away (from sb/sth). NOT for: going near.
typical: keep sb/sth away (from sth). NOT for: letting in.
Keep the children away from the fire.
keep from: prevent someone from doing something or something from happening
typical: keep sb/sth from (doing) sth. NOT for: allowing.
His ex-wife kept him from seeing his children.
Put the pizza at the bottom to keep the cheese from burning.
typical: keep yourself from doing sth. NOT for: giving in.
I couldn't keep myself from laughing.
typical: keep sth from sb. NOT for: telling.
I kept it from my mother.
They kept the truth from him.
keep in: make someone stay in hospital because they are too ill to go home
typical: keep sb in. NOT for: letting go home.
They kept her in overnight for observation.
force a child to stay indoors as punishment (BrE)
typical: keep sb in (after school). NOT for: letting out.
The teacher kept us in at lunchtime.
He was kept in for talking.
keep off: verb
prevent something from touching or harming something
typical: keep sth off (sth). NOT for: covering with it.
She held a cloth over them to keep the rain off.
How do we keep the flies off this food?
verb
not go on something, or tell someone to stay away
typical: keep off the grass, keep your hands off sth. NOT for: walking on it.
Keep off the grass.
Keep your hands off me!
verb
avoid eating or drinking something bad for you
typical: keep off sth, keep (sb) off sth. NOT for: indulging.
I'm trying to keep off alcohol.
The doctor told her to keep off fatty food.
verb
avoid a topic or subject
typical: keep off a subject. NOT for: bringing it up.
Let's keep off politics.
Try to keep off the subject of money.
keep on: verb
continue doing something, or do it many times
typical: keep on doing sth. NOT for: stopping.
You just have to keep on trying.
He kept on asking questions.
verb
continue to employ someone
typical: keep sb on. NOT for: firing.
They might keep you on after Christmas.
The firm kept on ten staff.
verb
talk about something in an annoying way (BrE informal)
typical: keep on (about sth). NOT for: staying silent.
There's no need to keep on about it.
She keeps on at me.
verb
continue to move in the same direction
typical: keep on going/walking. NOT for: turning back.
Keep on until you reach the lights.
He kept on walking.
keep out: stay outside a place, or prevent someone from entering
typical: keep out (of sth), keep sb out. NOT for: letting in.
typical: keep out (of sth). NOT for: getting involved.
I tried to keep out of the argument.
protect from something, such as weather or noise
typical: keep the rain/noise out. NOT for: letting in.
Heavy curtains keep the noise out.
The roof keeps the rain out.
keep out of: not enter a place, or prevent someone from entering it
typical: keep (sb) out of sth. NOT for: entering.
Keep children out of the garage.
typical: keep out of trouble/an argument. NOT for: getting involved.
She kept out of the argument.
keep up: verb
continue doing something
typical: keep up the good work, keep sth up. NOT for: stopping.
I can't keep this up any longer.
Keep up the good work!
verb
go as fast as someone else
typical: keep up (with sb). NOT for: falling behind.
I had to walk fast to keep up with him.
He ran too fast for me to keep up.
verb
stay informed about new facts or developments
typical: keep up with the news/technology. NOT for: reading old news.
Doctors must keep up with new research.
I try to keep up with the news.
verb
make something stay at its present level
typical: keep sth up (the pressure/prices). NOT for: reducing.
The government kept up the pressure.
They kept up prices to stay profitable.
kick off: verb
start (a meeting, event or football game)
typical: a game/event kicks off, kick off with sth. NOT for: finishing.
The match kicks off at noon.
The series kicked off with an interview.
verb
start a discussion, meeting or event
typical: kick sth off (with sth). NOT for: closing.
Would you care to kick off, Marion?
I'm going to kick off with a few remarks.
verb
remove someone from a team or group (informal)
typical: kick sb off (a team/committee). NOT for: admitting.
Joe was kicked off the committee for stealing funds.
She was kicked off the team.
verb
suddenly become angry or violent (BrE informal)
typical: things kick off, kick off about sth. NOT for: staying calm.
Trouble kicked off outside the pub.
He kicked off about the bill.
kick out: force someone to leave a place, job or organization
typical: kick sb out (of sth). NOT for: welcoming.
He was kicked out of the golf club.
knock down: verb
hit or push someone so that they fall
typical: knock sb down. NOT for: helping up.
Something hit him from behind and knocked him down.
He was knocked down in the crowd.
verb
hit someone with a vehicle so they are hurt or killed
typical: be knocked down by a car. NOT for: avoiding.
A child was knocked down by a car.
She was knocked down at the crossing.
verb
destroy a building or part of a building
typical: knock sth down, knock down a wall. NOT for: building.
They are knocking the old house down.
We knocked down a wall.
verb
reduce a price (informal)
typical: knock sth down (to + price). NOT for: raising.
I knocked him down to £50.
The shop knocked the price down.
knock out: verb
make someone unconscious or send them to sleep
typical: knock sb out, knock yourself out. NOT for: waking.
The champion knocked Biggs out in the seventh round.
The medicine totally knocked me out.
verb
defeat a team or person so they cannot continue in a competition
typical: knock sb/sth out (of sth). NOT for: qualifying.
Spain knocked Italy out of the cup.
He was knocked out in the first round.
verb
damage something so that it stops working
typical: knock sth out. NOT for: repairing.
The storm knocked out the power.
The strike knocked out phone lines.
verb
impress someone very much (informal)
typical: be knocked out by sth. NOT for: disappointing.
I was knocked out by her voice.
The view will knock you out.
knock over: hit something so that it falls over
typical: knock sth over. NOT for: setting upright.
The dog knocked over the lamp.
hit someone with a vehicle so they are hurt or killed
typical: be knocked over by a bus. NOT for: avoiding.
A woman was knocked over by a bus.
He was knocked over on the road.
rob a place such as a shop or bank (AmE informal)
typical: knock over a bank/store. NOT for: guarding.
knuckle down: suddenly start working or studying hard (informal)
typical: knuckle down (to sth). NOT for: relaxing.
If he doesn't knuckle down soon, he'll fail.
He is ready to knuckle down to the task.
